Engage leadership to foster commitment and accountability in implementing quality assurance measures. 3. Establish a national coordination team dedicated to overseeing the quality assurance of point-of-care testing. 4. Clearly define roles and responsibilities for all stakeholders involved in the quality assurance process. 5. Develop or review policies and integrate quality assurance into the national healthcare plan. 6. Define and implement standards to ensure the quality of point-of-care testing. 7. Conduct a thorough situation analysis to identify gaps and opportunities in the current testing framework. 8. Develop and implement a comprehensive plan to address identified needs and improve testing quality. 9. Plan for the allocation of financial and human resources to support quality assurance activities. 10. Select and assess sites for their suitability to conduct point-of-care testing. 11. Choose appropriate diagnostic products that meet quality and operational requirements. Phase 3: Evaluate, Improve, and Sustain Quality Assurance for HIV-Related Point-of-Care Testing 1. Conduct post-market surveillance to monitor the performance and safety of diagnostic products. 2. Utilize monitoring data to inform decision-making and improve testing processes. 3. Advocate for and communicate best practices in quality assurance to stakeholders. 4. Promote social entrepreneurship and public-private partnerships to enhance testing services. 5. Increase country ownership of quality assurance programs to ensure sustainability. 6. Conduct operational research to identify and address challenges in quality assurance implementation. Quality Assurance Cycle for Improving the Accuracy of Point-of-Care Testing The quality assurance cycle emphasizes the continuous and iterative nature of quality improvement and assessment. It is not a one-time activity but an ongoing process. The cycle includes three phases: planning and defining (Phase 1), implementing and monitoring (Phase 2), and evaluating and improving (Phase 3). These phases feed back into each other to ensure sustained quality improvement. Activities such as policy development may take time and should not delay the implementation of quality improvement measures. Strengthening and Expanding Laboratory and Diagnostic Services 1. Develop national laboratory strategic plans and policies to guide diagnostic services. 2. Evaluate diagnostic tools for performance and operational characteristics before their introduction. 3. Strategically plan the placement and harmonization of testing platforms to ensure cost-effectiveness and appropriate use. 4. Expand laboratory networks to support decentralized and integrated testing services, ensuring access to diagnostics even in remote areas. 5. Allocate sufficient resources, including financial and human, to maintain the availability of testing services. 6. Provide guidance on operations and service delivery, including specimen referral systems that ensure safe and efficient transport of samples and timely reporting of results. Increasing Access to HIV Viral Load Testing Viral load testing is recommended for monitoring treatment response and diagnosing treatment failure. Dried blood spot samples can be used to expand access to viral load testing, particularly in resource-limited settings. Strengthening existing laboratory services and expanding monitoring services in peripheral facilities are essential. Efforts should include leveraging early infant diagnosis (EID) networks, ensuring adequate infrastructure and technical expertise, and balancing centralized and point-of-care testing. Planning for the Transition from CD4 Count Testing to Viral Load Monitoring As viral load monitoring replaces CD4 count testing for treatment initiation and monitoring, the demand for CD4 testing will decrease. Programs should plan for a gradual reduction in CD4 testing capacity based on site-level demand, instrument age, and failure rates. Adequate sample referral networks for viral load testing must be established before scaling down CD4 testing. Financial planning should account for the transition, as cost savings may not be immediate due to increased per-test costs for CD4 testing as volumes decrease. CD4 testing will still be needed for baseline risk assessments and other clinical evaluations. Expanding Diagnostic Services to Point-of-Care Settings Decentralizing diagnostic services requires ensuring all aspects of testing are in place before implementation. This includes using high-quality, evaluated diagnostic tests, supervising and monitoring point-of-care testing, managing supply chains and equipment, and establishing data management systems for quality monitoring. Ensuring Appropriate Deployment of Diagnostic Technologies Strategic planning is essential to ensure that diagnostic technologies are deployed effectively, with adequate maintenance, trained personnel, and infrastructure in place. Maintenance and repair needs should be embedded in contractual agreements with manufacturers. Proper planning ensures that space and trained personnel are ready when equipment is delivered.
